title: Who Knew What Was in the Box — Epistemic Access, Secret Ritual Objects, Theory-of-Mind Asymmetries & Religious Authority

teenKit.tldr: Human brains naturally track what other people know or don't know, but treating supernatural beings like gods completely changes how we calculate hidden information. Secret boxes and rituals leverage this brain quirk to build power, authority, and awe.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how we model other people's minds reveals why rumors spread, how secrets create power dynamics, and why humans are wired to attribute all-knowing vision to invisible forces.
keyTakeaways: To guess what another person thinks is in a tricked-out box, your brain has to actively pause and suppress your own private knowledge.
Swapping an ordinary human for a divine figure shifts cognitive processing from standard perspective-taking to attributing omniscience.
Anthropologists and cognitive scientists use hidden objects and closed boxes to study how religions engineer secrecy and authority.

vocab.meaning: The brain's built-in software for figuring out that other people have thoughts, beliefs, and blind spots different from your own.
What a person is actually allowed to see, hear, or know based on their physical position or social status.
A situation where one person knows the real truth while another person is left working with outdated clues.
The hypothetical or theological trait of knowing absolutely everything that is happening, was happening, or will happen.

quiz.question: If you open a cracker box and find rocks inside, what makes guessing your mom's guess difficult?
options: You have to actively ignore the rocks you saw to simulate her blind spot
quiz.explanation: Your brain has to temporarily suppress your own direct reality to simulate what someone else sees from the outside.

quiz.question: What happens in the brain's logic when a researcher swaps out 'your mother' for 'God' in the box experiment?
options: It shifts from standard human perspective-taking to assuming total knowledge
It makes you forget what's actually in the box
quiz.explanation: Changing the target to an omniscient figure bypasses normal human perspective limitations.

quiz.question: Why do secret ritual objects often rely on hidden contents inside containers?
options: To keep them from melting in the sun
To control who has epistemic access and manufacture elite authority
Because boxes are cheap to manufacture
quiz.explanation: Controlling who gets to know what's inside a sacred box creates a powerful hierarchy of secret knowledge.
